steps.title: Beyond the five roles — two more, plus a look-alike
body: b1-u7 named five roles that take رَفْع or جَرّ or نَصْب: مُبْتَدَأ، خَبَر، فَاعِل، مَفْعُول بِهِ، مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ. Two more accusative-taking roles exist, and you've already been producing both correctly.

الْحَال describes a STATE at the exact moment of the verb — always accusative, always indefinite: رَجَعَ الرَّجُلُ سَعِيدًا ("the man returned happy") describes his state WHILE returning. Compare الرَّجُلُ سَعِيدٌ (a plain predicate, رَفْع, just a fact) — same word, different case, different meaning.

التَّمْيِيز specifies an ambiguous quantity — also always accusative, always indefinite: عِنْدِي عِشْرُونَ كِتَابًا ("I have twenty books") — عِشْرُونَ alone doesn't say twenty of what; كِتَابًا specifies it. This is the exact ending gr:numbers-11-99 already taught, just named now.

One look-alike, with an honest caveat: لَا النَّافِيَة لِلْجِنْس ("لَا that negates a whole category") also produces a word that LOOKS accusative — لَا مَاءَ فِي الْحَقِيبَةِ ("there is absolutely no water in the bag"). But a single-word اسم لا like مَاءَ is technically مَبْنِي (built), not truly مُعْرَب (declined) — it just happens to be written the same way. The full مُعْرَب/مَبْنِي distinction is its own future topic.

steps.title: Four sentences, two roles, one look-alike
steps.intro: Read each sentence and notice which accusative-looking word is doing what job. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: الْحَال — a state, not a fact
steps.prompt: What role does سَعِيدًا play, and why is it accusative?

options.label: الْحَال — describes the man's state while returning
خَبَر — states a fact about the man
مَفْعُول بِهِ — the object of the verb

steps.explanation: سَعِيدًا is indefinite and accusative, describing a temporary state during the verb's action — that's الْحَال, not a predicate (which would be nominative, سَعِيدٌ) or an object (رَجَعَ takes no object here).

steps.title: The same word, two cases, two meanings
steps.prompt: Both describe the student as sad. What's the real difference?

options.label: حَزِينًا (accusative) ties the sadness to the moment of coming; حَزِينٌ (nominative) just states a fact
They mean exactly the same thing
حَزِينًا is a mistake — it should be حَزِينٌ

steps.explanation: Case carries real meaning here: حَزِينًا (الْحَال) ties the sadness to the specific moment of coming; حَزِينٌ (خَبَر) just states he's sad, with no verb or moment attached at all.

steps.title: التَّمْيِيز — specifying a quantity
steps.prompt: What role does كِتَابًا play here?
steps.explanation: عِشْرُونَ alone doesn't say twenty of what — كِتَابًا (التَّمْيِيز) specifies it. You've been producing this exact ending correctly since gr:numbers-11-99.

steps.title: Looks accusative — but is it?
steps.prompt: مَاءَ ends in fatḥa here. Is it truly مَنْصُوب (case-marked accusative), like الْحَال or التَّمْيِيز?

options.label: Not exactly — it's مَبْنِي (built) with لَا, just written the way a منصوب noun would be
Yes — exactly the same mechanism as الْحَال or التَّمْيِيز
No — it has no case, and no position, at all

steps.explanation: A single-word اسم لا (like مَاءَ, with no إِضَافَة) is مَبْنِي — grammatically built together with لَا — not truly declined. It's written with a fatḥa either way, so it LOOKS like a normal accusative noun, but the underlying mechanism differs. The full مُعْرَب/مَبْنِي distinction is a future topic.

steps.title: Seven accusative-taking roles, one honest exception
steps.message: مُبْتَدَأ، خَبَر، فَاعِل، مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ (b1-u7) plus مَفْعُول بِهِ، الْحَال، التَّمْيِيز — every noun-role this project names now covers most of what shows up in an ordinary sentence. لَا النَّافِيَة لِلْجِنْس's مَبْنِي exception, and the full مُعْرَب/مَبْنِي distinction behind it, are still ahead.
